relationship.target: ILO 1: Demonstrate a clear understanding of the course structure, expectations, and key programming concepts in Java, including how these skills align with real- world IT challenges and professional ethical standards. [CLO1]

stage1.label: PARTIALLY_ALIGNED
stage1.explanation: The ILO is about this week's orientation (course structure, expectations), so it is on topic. But it has four gaps. First, "Demonstrate a clear understanding" is vague and gives no observable performance. Second, it asks for "key programming concepts in Java" and for alignment with "real- world IT challenges and professional ethical standards", and the Week 1 content (orientation, requirements, objectives, grading and policies) teaches none of these. Third, the Bloom level is too high for an orientation. Fourth, it is too broad to guide teaching or assessment.

course.title: Computer Programming 1
course.description: This course introduces students to the vital role of computers and computer programmers in shaping modern society. It aims to foster a strong foundation in logical formulation techniques essential for programming, while promoting the development of good coding practices. Students will be taught the fundamentals of Java programming and explore significant real-world applications. In line with La Consolacion University Philippines' commitment to forming Christo-centric Catholic professionals , the course integrates Marian Augustinian values in each lesson, ensuring that students not only achieve intellectual growth but also cultivate moral and ethical responsibility in the digital age. This holistic approach nurtures individuals who contribute positively to society, embodying community, humility, and love of service , as exemplified by the Blessed Virgin Mary and Saint Augustine. By the end of the course, students will have created their own Java applications, demonstrating both technical proficiency and a sense of purpose rooted in their Catholic faith.

Collaborate effectively within multi-disciplinary and culturally diverse teams to develop Java- based programming solutions that address social challenges, demonstrating social responsibility and cultural sensitivity.
Demonstrate the Filipino- Catholic Augustinian Spirituality through value webbing.

relationship.target: ILO10: Demonstrate the Augustinian, Marian and missionary Christ- centered Spirituality through value webbing. [CLO 4]

stage1.label: NOT_ALIGNED
stage1.explanation: The source (Week 1 content) is a course orientation: course contents, requirements and activities, objectives, grading system and policies on absences, tardiness and examinations. The target ILO asks students to demonstrate Augustinian, Marian and missionary Christ-centered Spirituality through value webbing. (1) The ILO is not about this week's content: nothing in the orientation teaches or introduces spirituality or value webbing. (2) The verb 'Demonstrate' is observable, but the performance (value webbing) is not specified and nothing in the content prepares it. (3) A Demonstrating-level performance on spirituality is far above what an orientation week can teach. (4) The ILO brings in a skill, value webbing, that the content never teaches. It belongs to a later value-integration lesson or to the course CLO, not to the orientation. The ILO should be about the orientation content, such as the course objectives and requirements.

course.title: Systems Engineering
course.description: This course introduces students to the principles and practices of systems engineering, focusing on the analysis, design, and management of complex systems. Through a blend of theoretical concepts and practical applications, students learn how to approach and solve large-scale engineering problems involving multiple components, stakeholders, and operational constraints. Key topics include requirements analysis, systems design, integration, project management, and performance evaluation. Students will develop skills in modeling and optimizing systems that integrate people, processes, and technology. They will explore methods for ensuring that systems are efficient, reliable, and adaptable across various industries, such as manufacturing, healthcare, and logistics. This course prepares BSIE students to play a vital role in creating systems that maximize performance, minimize waste, and support organizational goals. Beyond technical knowledge, the course integrates Marian Augustinian values into each lesson, fostering the development of students as Christo-centric Catholic professionals. The curriculum not only aims for intellectual growth but also instills a commitment to ethical decision-making, social responsibility, and compassionate service. Students will be equipped with the knowledge and values necessary to thrive as professionals in the field of Industrial Engineering.

Develop the ability to identify and solve systems engineering challenges, making decisions that improve performance, enhance efficiency, and support sustainable practices across diverse industries.

relationship.target: ILO1: To develop skills in analysis and design of both analog and digital circuits [CLO1]

stage1.label: PARTIALLY_ALIGNED
stage1.explanation: The target ILO is related to the source content, but it has several gaps. (1) "To develop skills" is not an observable, assessable student performance; it names no action the student can show. (2) "both analog and digital circuits" is broader than the source content, which covers electronic systems, design of circuits and differential amplifiers (differential gain, common mode gain, CMRR, configurations) and teaches no digital circuit content. (3) The ILO names neither the differential amplifier topics nor the electronic system design topics the week actually teaches, so it is too vague to guide teaching and assessment. (4) "analysis and design" needs a stated object and expected evidence, and the history, notation and classification topics only support this at a lower level.

course.title: Fundamentals of Mixed Signals and Sensors
course.description: This course covers operational amplifiers, signal converters, power switching devices and the construction and operation of sensors and transducers for converting physical parameters into electrical signals and vice-versa. The course focuses on the application of these devices in developing signal conversion circuits that allows measurement, processing and control of physical parameters by digital processing systems such as a finite state machine or a digital computer. Topics on actuators are also included. Anchored in the Marian and Augustinian values of truth (veritas), unity (unitas), and charity (caritas), the course encourages students to design technology that promotes social responsibility, collaboration, and compassion. Through hands-on projects, learners will not only develop technical proficiency but also embody ethical stewardship — using their knowledge to create solutions that serve the needs of others and contribute to the common good.

clos.statement: Identify the design process of electronic circuits and systems and conduct experiments involving sensors and mixed-signal systems, analyze data, and interpret results to improve performance and reliability.

Develop analytical and design skills for both analog and digital electronic circuit and implement sensor-based systems that integrate hardware and software components while considering economic, environmental, and ethical constraints.

Analyze and apply the behavior of passive components in AC circuits and their instrumentation applications in multidisciplinary teams to design, test, and optimize mixed-signal and sensor applications for engineering solutions

Exhibit lifelong learning, precision, and ethical responsibility in performing measurements and calibration tasks. Engage in continuous learning by exploring emerging technologies and trends in sensors, instrumentation, and mixed-signal design for future innovation
